title: How to Make Time for 'Deep Work'
paragraphs: Emails, chat messages, meetings and notifications fill up the working day for many people. As a result, it can be very difficult to find time for "deep work," the kind of focused, uninterrupted work that produces our most valuable results.

The term "deep work" was made popular by the American computer science professor and author Cal Newport. It refers to work that requires full concentration, such as writing, solving complex problems or learning difficult new skills. It is the opposite of "shallow work," which includes tasks like answering emails or attending routine meetings. These tasks are necessary, but they do not usually require much thought.
So how can you make more time for deep work? Productivity experts suggest several strategies.

First, find out how you are actually spending your time. Experts suggest listing all the tasks you do during a typical week and calculating how much time you spend on deep work compared with shallow work. Many people are surprised by the results.

Second, schedule deep work in your calendar. Experts recommend treating it like an important meeting or a doctor's appointment, and planning other activities around it. Some people find it helpful to set aside a regular block of time at the same time every day, often in the morning.

Third, remove as many distractions as possible. Even a short interruption can break your concentration, and it may take some time to get back into a state of deep focus. During your focus time, you can turn on "do not disturb" mode on your devices, or close your email and messaging apps completely.

Finally, do not worry if you cannot find long periods of free time. According to some experts, one of the biggest misunderstandings about deep work is that you need a huge, uninterrupted block of time to make it worthwhile. Even shorter sessions of focused work can be valuable.
By protecting time for deep work, you may find that you can achieve more important results with less stress.
